Depends on the country, state, and city actually. In most states in the US, the general fund supplies most law enforcement non-budgeted overhead, which in turn is supplied by fines from tickets. It's usually two thirds to a half of the fine that go into this fund. So if there is an "Unexpected Cost", then that comes from the general fund at City or State level depending on the type of department.

There are departments that do get funding that depend on revenue stream of fines, usually in smaller towns or rural counties. Many larger cities have budget overruns constantly, and thus pull from the general fund to take care of cost. So yes, many departments do rely on tickets as a revenue stream, sometimes indirectly.

Then you have seizure of money, which has been a touchy subject, especially last year. This is were police pull you over, find cash they "suspect" is related to a crime and seize it for evidence. They don't even have to charge you, just have "suspicion" that your using it for something illegal. It's called "Civil Forfeiture" and there is plenty of incentive to have these suspicions, with departments able to keep up to "90%" of what they seize.
